article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Design LMSs with simple, interactive, familiar features to reduce anxiety and leverage self-efficacy mediation
description: The authors recommend that designers "integrate simple, interactive, and familiar features in the design of LMSs" and provide incentives to motivate usage, because positive learning experiences are more likely with LMSs that are easy to use and introduce the least anxieties. This assists diffusion via the mediating effect of computer self-efficacy. They also note a trade-off: easier interfaces may reduce effective task manipulation capabilities.
requirements: Designers must balance ease of navigation against effective task manipulation (the cognitive-cost/effective-usage ratio)
constraints: The more 'easy to use' the interface is designed, the less effective the features become, reducing LMS capabilities
target_learning_goals: supporting positive attitudes and ease of use perceptions in LMS-based learning
examples: The authors suggest it is feasible to build multiple LMS interfaces for students with different levels of computer self-efficacy
key_sources: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf

article_title: On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education
citation: Küchemann, S., Avila, K. E., Dinc, Y., Hortmann, C., Revenga, N., Ruf, V., Stausberg, N., Steinert, S., Fischer, F., Fischer, M., Kasneci, E., Kasneci, G., Kuhr, T., Kutyniok, G., Malone, S., Sailer, M., Schmidt, A., Stadler, M., Weller, J. & Kuhn, J. (2025). On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00301-w
title: Large multimodal foundation models (LMFMs) as LLM-enabled multimodal AI middleware for education
description: LMFMs are foundation models that, building on the LLM-as-middleware idea demonstrated by Shen and colleagues, process inputs and outputs not only via written text but also via spoken text, images, and videos, with examples ChatGPT-4-Turbo and Gemini. The review frames them as advancing personalized learning, engagement, and research tooling, while raising accuracy, bias, privacy, and access concerns. It characterizes them as representing "a significant advancement in this field due to its multimodality, boosted accuracy, faster response times". The framework organizes the article's four-audience analysis of opportunities and challenges.
requirements: Requires LLMs fine-tuned to the specifications of connected AI tools to generate correct inputs, per the middleware account.
Educational use requires reevaluation of teaching methods, curricula, and new competencies among educators and students, per the review.
constraints: Accuracy and reliability of outputs remain concerns; biases may be intensified by processing multiple input modalities.
The digital divide and resource limits of educational institutions constrain equitable implementation, per the review.
target_learning_goals: personalized multimodal learning support
formative feedback
representational competence
language learning
computational thinking
examples: The review describes LMFM capabilities including speech-to-text, image-to-text, text-to-image, and text-to-speech functionalities supporting barrier-free interaction for students with disabilities.
key_sources: Küchemann, S., Avila, K. E., Dinc, Y., Hortmann, C., Revenga, N., Ruf, V., Stausberg, N., Steinert, S., Fischer, F., Fischer, M., Kasneci, E., Kasneci, G., Kuhr, T., Kutyniok, G., Malone, S., Sailer, M., Schmidt, A., Stadler, M., Weller, J. & Kuhn, J. (2025). On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00301-w

article_title: On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education
citation: Küchemann, S., Avila, K. E., Dinc, Y., Hortmann, C., Revenga, N., Ruf, V., Stausberg, N., Steinert, S., Fischer, F., Fischer, M., Kasneci, E., Kasneci, G., Kuhr, T., Kutyniok, G., Malone, S., Sailer, M., Schmidt, A., Stadler, M., Weller, J. & Kuhn, J. (2025). On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00301-w
title: LMFM-supported learning mechanisms for learners: multimedia feedback, barrier-free interaction, scaffolded visual and code generation, collaboration support
description: The review enumerates a set of learning mechanisms LMFM applications can facilitate for students: multimodal formative feedback combining text and images, barrier-free interaction via speech-to-text and translation, real-time scaffolding during image, handwritten-solution, and code generation, representational competence training, animation of phenomena, targeted support during experimentation, collaborative learning via peer feedback models, and interpretation of behavioral and physiological data. It notes that "text in combination with images leads to better understanding than text alone". The pattern is a learner-facing ensemble of multimodal support functions around one LMFM application.
requirements: Effective preprompting to integrate animation principles and prevent hallucinations.
Domain-specific content provided to fine-tuned LMFMs for individualized applications.
Students need sufficient representational competence to critically reflect on LMFM-generated visual representations.
constraints: Benefits for complex or abstract concepts are framed as potential; the review states LMFMs 'could' and 'may' provide these supports rather than reporting tested gains.
target_learners: students with visual or auditory impairments or difficulties in writing or reading
target_learning_goals: understanding of complex or abstract concepts
representational competence
language skills
feedback during graph and code generation
self-regulated learning
examples: The review describes LMFMs analyzing images of experimental setups, generating artificial measurement data to reduce extraneous cognitive load during experimentation, and acting as conversational partners in history role-play as characters like Napoleon.

article_title: Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data.
citation: Urresti-Gundlach M., Tolks D., Kiessling C., Wagner-Menghin M., Härtl A., Hege I. (2017). Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1013-1
title: Collection of 66 online virtual patients in the CASUS system at LMU Munich
description: A collection of 66 online virtual patients provided as a self-directed learning module in the integrated internal medicine and operative medicine curriculum at LMU Munich, created with the CASUS® VP system by different authors and reviewed by a content matter expert and a medical educator. The VPs are "designed to match curricular objectives of common symptoms, train clinical reasoning skills, and complement the face-to-face courses."
requirements: Created with the CASUS® virtual patient system
Reviewed by a content matter expert and a medical educator
constraints: Authors were not specifically instructed to construct the VPs based on real patients or focus on common vs. rare diseases
target_learners: medical students in their second and third clinical terms
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning skills
common symptoms in internal medicine and operative medicine
examples: Used as a self-directed learning module complementing lectures, problem-based learning sessions, and bedside teaching
key_sources: Urresti-Gundlach M., Tolks D., Kiessling C., Wagner-Menghin M., Härtl A., Hege I. (2017). Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1013-1

article_title: Use of Computing Devices as Sensors to Measure Their Impact on Primary and Secondary Students' Performance.
citation: Fernández-Soriano Francisco Luis, López Belén, Martínez-España Raquel, Muñoz Andrés, Cantabella Magdalena. (2019). Use of Computing Devices as Sensors to Measure Their Impact on Primary and Secondary Students' Performance. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s19143226
title: LMS connection-log dataset in which computing devices act as sensors recording device type, operating system and connection habits
description: Connection-log dataset in which computing devices act as sensors recording each student's LMS accesses with timestamp, device type and operating system, together with student performance records for the academic year 2017/18. The sample splits into connectors and non-connectors: "1011 students (52.17%) have ever connected to the LMS, whereas 927 students (47.83%) have never been logged on." Logs also yield per-student login totals, weekly averages and most frequent connection day and time slot.
requirements: Students must be allowed to connect to the LMS with any computing device, and the logs must capture timestamp, device type and operating system for each access.
constraints: No control group could be created for the study due to legal reasons raised by the school.
Phablets and Chrome OS are marginal in the sample and their results are not conclusive.
target_learners: Students from Fourth Grade (9-to-10-year-olds) to the last year of bachelor's degree (17-to-18-year-olds) in a Spanish school network
target_learning_goals: Relating computing-device LMS access patterns to students' academic performance in passed and failed subjects
examples: The school lent 192 iPads, and students could borrow a device already available in the school.
key_sources: Fernández-Soriano Francisco Luis, López Belén, Martínez-España Raquel, Muñoz Andrés, Cantabella Magdalena. (2019). Use of Computing Devices as Sensors to Measure Their Impact on Primary and Secondary Students' Performance. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s19143226

article_title: Learning Mechanics and Game Mechanics Under the Perspective of Self-Determination Theory to Foster Motivation in Digital Game Based Learning
citation: Proulx, J. N., Romero, M., & Arnab, S. (2017). Learning Mechanics and Game Mechanics Under the Perspective of Self-Determination Theory to Foster Motivation in Digital Game Based Learning. Simulation & Gaming. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878116674399
title: The LMGM-SDT framework combines the LM-GM mapping model with self-determination theory to analyze motivation in digital game based learning
description: The article introduces the LMGM-SDT theoretical framework, created by "mixing together the LM-GM classification based on Bloom's taxonomy from Arnab et al. (2015) and the self-determination continuum from Ryan and Deci (2009)". It classifies game mechanics and learning mechanics along the self-determination continuum (horizontal axis, from amotivation to intrinsic motivation) and Bloom's thinking-skill levels (vertical axis, from retention to creating), so that designers can evaluate both the pedagogical outcome and the motivational potential of each mechanic. The framework aims to "overcome the motivational limits of games and to contribute to a better analysis of the motivational factors of DGBL".
requirements: the framework requires identifying learning mechanics and game mechanics with a clearer link to the SDT components of the self-determination continuum
constraints: the framework has not yet been tested in a concrete class setting
some mechanics, such as the meta-game mechanic and realism mechanic, cannot be classified due to their neutral motivational potential
target_learners: learners using digital game based learning across educational levels
target_learning_goals: fostering learners' autonomous motivation and engagement in DGBL
examples: the authors classify game and learning mechanics such as collaboration, competition, progression, and feedback into columns of the self-determination continuum in Figure 3 and Table 2
key_sources: Proulx, J. N., Romero, M., & Arnab, S. (2017). Learning Mechanics and Game Mechanics Under the Perspective of Self-Determination Theory to Foster Motivation in Digital Game Based Learning. Simulation & Gaming. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878116674399

article_title: Learning Mechanics and Game Mechanics Under the Perspective of Self-Determination Theory to Foster Motivation in Digital Game Based Learning
citation: Proulx, J. N., Romero, M., & Arnab, S. (2017). Learning Mechanics and Game Mechanics Under the Perspective of Self-Determination Theory to Foster Motivation in Digital Game Based Learning. Simulation & Gaming. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878116674399
title: LM-GM mapping model: mapping learning mechanics to game mechanics for serious game design and analysis
description: The Learning Mechanics and Game Mechanics (LM-GM) model from Lim et al. (2013), evaluated by Arnab et al. (2015) as a serious game analysis guideline, maps pedagogical constructs to entertaining gameplay. Pedagogical elements are viewed as "an abstract interface while game elements are deemed as a concrete interface of SGs". The model can be used to either aid serious game design or game analysis, and the article merges it with the Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics (MDA) model to combine pedagogical and entertainment attributes of gameplay.
requirements: the model is descriptive and not prescriptive, "in the sense that it allows its users to freely relate learning and gaming mechanics to describe SG situations by drawing a map and filling a table"
constraints: reusability is a key challenge because serious games can be bespoke and not immediately re-purposable, as the article reports citing Arnab and Clarke (2016)
target_learners: designers and analysts of serious games
learners in classroom settings using serious games
target_learning_goals: linking ludic elements to pedagogical intent through players' actions and gameplay
examples: the model informed the design of the PR:EPARe game for relationship and sex education discourse, and supported the definition of key SGM reuse principles from the PR:EPARe and Seconds games
key_sources: Proulx, J. N., Romero, M., & Arnab, S. (2017). Learning Mechanics and Game Mechanics Under the Perspective of Self-Determination Theory to Foster Motivation in Digital Game Based Learning. Simulation & Gaming. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878116674399

article_title: How to Survive a Learning Management System (LMS) Implementation? A Stakeholder Analysis Approach
citation: Ajayi Ekuase-Anwansedo, Susannah F. Craig, Jose Noguera. (2018). How to Survive a Learning Management System (LMS) Implementation? A Stakeholder Analysis Approach. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=How+to+Survive+a+Learning+Management+System+Implementation+A+Stakeholder+Analysis+Approach
title: Four-role classification of stakeholders in the LMS implementation process
description: The article classifies LMS implementation stakeholders by their current role in the process into four groups: "I. Decision-making stakeholders II. End-user stakeholders III. Vendor stakeholders IV. Support stakeholders". Decision-making stakeholders (administration, the CIO, and faculty representatives) decide on and fund the implementation; end users are faculty and students; vendors create or sell the LMS; support stakeholders assist users. The article notes roles overlap, e.g. faculty may be end user, decision maker, and student support simultaneously.
requirements: Stakeholders must be identified and classified by their current role in the implementation process for the typology to guide engagement
constraints: Roles often overlap, so a single stakeholder may occupy more than one category
target_learning_goals: successful adoption and use of a learning management system to support teaching and learning
examples: Figure 2 depicts the stakeholder types and their roles in the LMS implementation process
key_sources: Ajayi Ekuase-Anwansedo, Susannah F. Craig, Jose Noguera. (2018). How to Survive a Learning Management System (LMS) Implementation? A Stakeholder Analysis Approach. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=How+to+Survive+a+Learning+Management+System+Implementation+A+Stakeholder+Analysis+Approach

article_title: Education dimensions of MGI: a question of multidisciplinarity, purpose, and equality
citation: Eva M. Campo. (2014). Education dimensions of MGI: a question of multidisciplinarity, purpose, and equality. https://doi.org/10.1557/opl.2013.779
title: Lab-to-Market-to-Classroom (LMC) continuum with the theory-experiment-data intersection as the conceptual and content framework of the MGI
description: The paper proposes the LMC continuum as a classroom model in which practical, hands-on content of high student interest is not only delivered but also generated and end-consumer tested, creating a social ecosystem representative of society at large. It positions the intersection of the theory-experiment-data content framework and the lab-market-classroom conceptual framework as the zone where the MGI will unfold. The paper states that the LMC builds on student-centered education and active, project-based learning.
requirements: Topics and systems under study must be real problems and of specific interest to the students
constraints: Implementation within the K-12 segment is strained by the need for whole school reform under the PBL paradigm
target_learning_goals: Multidisciplinary competence in materials science combining theory, experiment, and data science
Twenty-first-century skills and workforce preparation
examples: The Spring 2013 MRS Education Symposium 'Towards a Lab-to-Classroom' gave rise to the lab-to-classroom concept, and the MGI has identified the classroom as a component of the MGI framework.
key_sources: Eva M. Campo. (2014). Education dimensions of MGI: a question of multidisciplinarity, purpose, and equality. https://doi.org/10.1557/opl.2013.779

article_title: Education dimensions of MGI: a question of multidisciplinarity, purpose, and equality
citation: Eva M. Campo. (2014). Education dimensions of MGI: a question of multidisciplinarity, purpose, and equality. https://doi.org/10.1557/opl.2013.779
title: First LMC program: refreshable, photo-actuatable tactile displays for the visually impaired
description: As a proof of concept for the LMC approach at the K-12 segment, the paper describes the first LMC program, designed for the dissemination of refreshable, photo-actuatable tactile displays to the visually impaired, serving both lab-to-market and lab-to-classroom initiatives. Through programmatic design via the logic model, the overlap among classroom, market, and laboratory was predicted to nucleate when a technology in developmental phase is deployed in a classroom with high affinity to such technology.
requirements: Deployment in a classroom with high affinity to the technology in developmental phase
target_learning_goals: Student competence in twenty-first-century skills through hands-on, real-problem project work
examples: Students act as stakeholders who help decide both content and applications to be included in the developing curriculum and provide technology feedback.
key_sources: Eva M. Campo. (2014). Education dimensions of MGI: a question of multidisciplinarity, purpose, and equality. https://doi.org/10.1557/opl.2013.779
